# English Grammar and Usage for the CRT

> **What UPSC asks on this**
> 1. **Spot the error**: a sentence split into three parts plus "No error". The fault is almost always agreement, tense, preposition, article or pronoun.
> 2. **Fill in the blank**: the right preposition, article, verb form or paired conjunction.
> 3. **Transformation**: active to passive, direct to indirect speech, sometimes degree of comparison.
> 4. **Vocabulary**: synonym, antonym, idiom or phrase, one-word substitution, confused word pair.
> 5. **Sentence improvement** and **sentence or paragraph rearrangement**.
> 6. **Short reading comprehension** passage with a few questions on facts, inference and tone.

## How the English section behaves

**Summary: the marks come from a small set of rules applied to ordinary sentences, so learn the rules, not the sentences.**

The syllabus line is "Hindi and English language skills". In UPSC Recruitment Test papers that carry a General Ability Test, the English questions are short, objective and rule-based. They test whether you recognise correct usage, not whether you can name grammatical terms.

Negative marking is one-third of the question's marks. In error spotting, if two parts are definitely correct, choose between the remaining part and "No error". "No error" is sometimes the key, so do not force a correction where nothing is wrong. Use this order of checks:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Read the whole sentence] --> B[Find subject and verb]
    B --> C[Check number agreement]
    C --> D[Check tense and time words]
    D --> E[Check preposition pairs]
    E --> F[Check article and noun]
    F --> G[Check pronoun and comparison]
    G --> H[All pass means No error]
```

## Subject–verb agreement

**Summary: find the real subject, ignore everything between it and the verb, then match number.**

Why the rule exists: English marks number only in the present tense and in *was/were*, so the examiner hides the subject behind a phrase to see whether you can still find it.

- **Words between subject and verb do not count.** "The Principal, **along with** the teachers, **is** attending." The same holds for *as well as, together with, with, in addition to, accompanied by, no less than, like, besides, except*.
- **Two subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb**, unless they name one person or one idea. "The Vice Principal and the DDO **are** present" (two people), but "The Vice Principal and DDO **is** present" (one person holding both charges). "Bread and butter **is** his breakfast."
- **Either...or, neither...nor, or, not only...but also: the verb agrees with the nearer subject.** "Neither the Principal nor the teachers **were** present." "Neither the teachers nor the Principal **was** present."
- **Each, every, everyone, anyone, nobody, either, neither, many a, more than one** take a singular verb. "Each of the students **has** a copy." "Many a teacher **has** asked." "More than one section **was** affected."
- **A number of + plural noun takes a plural verb; the number of takes a singular verb.** "A number of teachers **have** applied." "The number of applicants **is** large."
- **Collective nouns** (*staff, committee, team, class, jury, government*) are singular when the group acts as one: "The committee **has** submitted **its** report." They are plural only when members act separately: "The committee **were** divided in their opinion." A mix such as "The committee **have** submitted **its** report" is wrong.
- **Fractions and quantity words take the number of the noun after "of"**: "Half of the work **is** done." "Half of the students **are** present." Same for *most of, some of, all of, a lot of, plenty of, the rest of*.
- **Sums, distances and periods counted as one amount are singular**: "Five thousand rupees **is** the fee." "Three hours **is** enough for the paper."
- **Relative pronouns carry the number of their antecedent**: "She is one of the teachers who **have** been selected" (*who* points to *teachers*). But "She is the **only one** of the teachers who **has** been selected." "It is I who **am** responsible."
- **Here/There + verb: look at the noun after the verb**: "There **are** two vacancies." "Here **is** the file."
- **Plural in form, singular in meaning**: *news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics, measles, the United States*. "Mathematics **is** compulsory." Always plural: *scissors, trousers, spectacles, premises, police, cattle, people, children, alms, thanks, proceeds, belongings*. "The police **have** arrived."

School example: a notice reads "The list of selected candidates are displayed." The subject is *list*, not *candidates*: "The list ... **is** displayed."

Memory aid: **"Along with" leaves the first subject alone.** Only **"and"** adds a subject; every other joining phrase is ignored.

## Nouns and pronouns

**Summary: uncountable nouns have no plural and no "a", and pronoun case depends on the job the pronoun does.**

- **Uncountable nouns**: *advice, information, furniture, luggage, baggage, news, scenery, poetry, hair, equipment, stationery, machinery, homework, evidence, progress, knowledge, bread*. Never "an advice", "informations", "furnitures", "equipments". Count them with a unit: "a piece of advice", "two items of furniture".
- **Foreign plurals** UPSC likes: criterion → **criteria**, phenomenon → **phenomena**, datum → **data**, medium → **media**, curriculum → **curricula**, syllabus → **syllabi/syllabuses**, alumnus → **alumni**, memorandum → **memoranda**, formula → **formulae/formulas**, index → **indices**, basis → **bases**, analysis → **analyses**. "The criteria **are** clear" but "The criterion **is** clear."
- **Number words used as adjectives stay singular**: "a **two-hour** test", "a **five-year** plan", "a **ten-rupee** note", "**two hundred** students". Plural only when used as nouns: "hundreds of students".
- **Possessive**: use *'s* for living things and for time or distance ("a **week's** leave", "a **day's** work"); use *of* for objects ("the leg **of** the table").
- **Pronoun case**: object case after prepositions and verbs: "between you and **me**", "Let him and **me** go". After *than/as* use the case the full clause needs: "She is taller than **I** (am)"; "He helped me more than (he helped) **her**."
- **Order of persons**: second, third, first in ordinary sentences (**231**: "You, he and I"); first, second, third when admitting a fault (**123**: "I, you and he are to blame").
- **Reflexive verbs** need *oneself*: *avail oneself of, absent oneself from, enjoy oneself, pride oneself on, apply oneself to, exert oneself*. "He absented **himself** from duty." "She availed **herself of** the opportunity."
- **Each other** for two, **one another** for more than two (the exam rule).
- **Who/whom/which/that**: *whom* is the object ("the teacher **whom** we met"); *which* for things; *that* after superlatives and after *all, same, only, any, nothing*: "the best school **that** I know".
- **Antecedent agreement**: "Every student must bring **his or her** identity card." "Each of the girls has **her** own locker." Exam English does not accept *their* for a singular antecedent.

School example: "The staff has submitted **their** reports" is wrong because *staff* is singular here. Write "**its** reports" or recast as "The staff members have submitted their reports."

## Tenses and conditionals

**Summary: time words decide the tense, and the earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.**

- **Present perfect never sits with a finished-time word.** "I **met** him yesterday" (not *have met*). *Yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago* need the simple past. *Just, already, yet, ever, never, so far, since, for* go with the present perfect.
- **Since + point of time; for + length of time.** "She has been working here **since 2018**" or "**for seven years**." With *since* the main verb is in a perfect tense.
- **Past perfect** for the action that happened first: "The bell **had rung** before the students **entered**." With only one past action, use the simple past.
- **Time clauses take the present, not the future**: "When the DEO **comes**, I **will** inform you." Same after *as soon as, till, until, before, after, unless, if*.
- **Conditionals** (never *would* in the if-clause):

| Type | If-clause | Main clause |
|---|---|---|
| Real (open) | simple present | will + verb |
| Unreal present | simple past (were) | would + verb |
| Unreal past | past perfect | would have + V3 |

"If I **were** the Principal, I **would** change the timetable." "If he **had studied**, he **would have passed**." Wrong: "If he would have studied."

- **Stative verbs avoid the continuous**: *know, believe, understand, own, belong, want, like, hate, prefer, seem, contain*. "I **know** the answer" (not *am knowing*).
- **Sequence of tenses**: a past main verb pulls the subordinate verb into the past: "He said that he **was** ill." Exception: universal truths and habits stay present: "He said that the earth **revolves** round the sun."
- **Paired conjunctions**: *no sooner ... than; hardly/scarcely ... when; not only ... but also; both ... and; either ... or; neither ... nor; lest ... should; so ... that; such ... that*. "**No sooner** had the bell rung **than** the students rushed out." "**Hardly** had I reached **when** it started raining."
- **Unless** already contains *not*: "Unless you work hard, you will fail" (not *unless you do not*).
- **Used to / be used to**: "She **used to teach** Hindi" (past habit) but "She **is used to teaching** Hindi" (accustomed; *-ing* form).

Memory aid: **"Since the point, for the period."** **"If never takes would."**

## Articles

**Summary: a/an go by sound, "the" goes by definiteness, and some nouns take no article at all.**

- **a/an by the first sound, not the first letter**: *an hour, an honest man, an heir, an MLA, an FIR, an NGO, an X-ray, an SMC meeting*; *a university, a European, a one-rupee note, a union, a useful book, a hotel*.
- **"The"** with: superlatives and ordinals (*the best, the first*); unique things (*the sun, the sky*); rivers, seas, mountain ranges, deserts and island groups (*the Yamuna, the Himalayas, the Thar, the Andamans*); plural or descriptive country names (*the Netherlands, the USA, the UAE*); newspapers and holy books (*The Hindu, the Gita*); musical instruments (*play the harmonium*); adjectives used as nouns (*the poor, the blind*); famous buildings and ships (*the Red Fort, the Qutub Minar*); *the same, the only, the whole*.
- **No article** with: languages (*Hindi, English*); meals (*breakfast*); most diseases (*fever, cancer*); uncountable nouns used generally (*information, advice*); subjects (*mathematics*); *school, college, hospital, church, bed, prison, court* used for their purpose ("go to **school**", but "went to **the** school to meet the Principal").
- **A/an in a rate sense**: "twice **a** week", "Rs 500 **a** month".
- **One article for one person, two for two**: "the Principal and Secretary" (one person); "the Principal and the Secretary" (two).

School example: "She is a MLA's daughter" is wrong because MLA begins with the sound /em/: "**an** MLA's daughter".

## Prepositions

**Summary: most preposition questions test a fixed pair, so learn the pairs as units.**

Verbs that take **no preposition** (the trap is to add one): *discuss (about), enter (into) a room, reach (to), resemble (to), order (for), attack (on), accompany (with), answer (to), approach (to), comprise (of), emphasise (on), stress (on), request (for), marry (with), obey (to)*. Some related phrases and noun forms do take one: *enter into* an agreement (a different sense of the verb), *lay emphasis on*, *a request for*.

Pairs that change meaning:

| Pair | Use |
|---|---|
| agree **with** / agree **to** | with a person / to a proposal |
| differ **with** / differ **from** | with a person in opinion / from a thing in nature |
| angry **with** / angry **at** | with a person / at a thing |
| die **of** / die **from** | of a disease / from a wound or cause |
| compare **with** / compare **to** | same kind / unlike things (metaphor) |
| between / among | two / more than two |
| by / till | deadline ("by Monday") / continuing ("till Monday") |
| in time / on time | early enough / exactly punctual |
| beside / besides | next to / in addition to |
| at / on / in (time) | clock time / day and date / month, year, season |

Other fixed phrases: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable* **to**; *prefer* tea **to** coffee; *good at*; *fond of*; *afraid of*; *capable of*; *accused of*; *charged with*; *blame for*; *insist on*; *depend on*; *rely on*; *succeed in*; *suffer from*; *consist of*; *in accordance with*; *according to*; *despite* (never *despite of*); *in spite of*; *sympathy for*; *sympathise with*; *indifferent to*; *different from*; *married to*; *divided into* parts; *divided among* three people.

School example: "The DDO insisted on me to sign the register" becomes "insisted on **my signing**" or "insisted **that I sign**".

## Adjectives, adverbs and comparison

**Summary: compare like with like, use the right degree for the count, and exclude the thing itself with "other".**

- **Comparative for two, superlative for three or more**: "Of the two sections, XII-A is the **better**." "Of all the sections, XII-A is the **best**."
- **"Than any other"**: "Delhi has more government schools than **any other** city." Without *other*, Delhi is compared with itself.
- **Latin comparatives take "to", not "than"**: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior* (and the verb *prefer*). "He is senior **to** me."
- **Double comparison is wrong**: "more better", "most tallest".
- **Absolute adjectives have no degree**: *unique, perfect, complete, round, square, dead, universal*. Not "more unique".
- **Elder/eldest** for family members and never with *than*; **older/oldest** everywhere else. "My elder brother is older than I."
- **Fewer** for countable, **less** for uncountable: "fewer students", "less time". **Many/much** split the same way. **Few** = hardly any, **a few** = some, **the few** = all the small number there is; *little, a little, the little* do the same job for uncountables.
- **Adverbs**: *hard* (with effort) vs *hardly* (scarcely); *late* vs *lately* (recently). "He works **hard**" and "He **hardly** works" are opposites. Put *only* next to the word it limits: "**Only** she attended" vs "She attended **only** the first session."
- **Enough** follows an adjective but precedes a noun: "good **enough**", "**enough** time".
- **Verbs of sense take adjectives**: "The soup tastes **good**", "She looks **happy**".
- **Comparison of equals**: *as ... as*; in the negative *so ... as* is also correct.

Memory aid for the "to" group: **S-J-S-I-P-P** (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer) all point **to**.

## Active and passive voice

**Summary: the object moves to the front, the verb becomes be + past participle in the same tense, and the doer goes after "by".**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Find the object] --> B[Make it the subject]
    B --> C[Add be in same tense]
    C --> D[Add past participle V3]
    D --> E[Add by plus doer]
    E --> F[Drop obvious doer]
```

| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Present simple | teaches | is/are taught |
| Present continuous | is teaching | is/are being taught |
| Present perfect | has taught | has/have been taught |
| Past simple | taught | was/were taught |
| Past continuous | was teaching | was/were being taught |
| Past perfect | had taught | had been taught |
| Future simple | will teach | will be taught |
| Modal | can/must teach | can/must be taught |

Perfect continuous tenses and the future continuous are not normally put into the passive.

- **Imperatives**: "Shut the door." → "Let the door **be shut**." "Please help the new students." → "You **are requested to** help the new students." "Keep the lab clean." → "The lab **should be kept** clean."
- **Questions**: "Who taught you?" → "**By whom** were you taught?" "Did she submit the report?" → "**Was** the report submitted by her?"
- **Two objects**: "The Principal gave the students prizes." → "The students were given prizes" or "Prizes were given to the students."
- **Prepositional verbs keep the preposition**: "The class laughed at him." → "He was laughed **at** by the class."
- **Drop the agent** when it is obvious or unknown: "Someone has stolen my bag." → "My bag has been stolen."
- **Some passives take a different preposition**: *known to, surprised at, pleased with, interested in, satisfied with*. "Everyone knows him." → "He is known **to** everyone."

## Direct and indirect speech

**Summary: when the reporting verb is in the past, shift the tense back, change the pronouns, and change words of time and place.**

Why the rule exists: the reported words were spoken at an earlier time and place, so every marker of "here and now" must move.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Is reporting verb past] --> B[Yes: shift tense back]
    A --> C[No: keep tense]
    B --> D[Change pronouns]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Change time and place words]
    E --> F[Statement: add that]
    E --> G[Question: if or wh-word]
    E --> H[Command: to-infinitive]
```

- **Tense shift** (past reporting verb): present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; past simple → past perfect; *will* → *would*; *shall* → *should*; *can* → *could*; *may* → *might*; *must* → *had to*. Past perfect and *would, could, should, might, ought to* do not change.
- **No shift** when the reporting verb is present or future ("He says that he **is** busy"), and for universal truths, habits and proverbs ("The teacher said that water **boils** at 100 degrees").
- **Words that change**: now → then; today → that day; tonight → that night; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; ago → before; here → there; this → that; these → those; last week → the previous week; next year → the following year.
- **Statements**: *said to* → *told*; add *that*. "He said to me, 'I am busy.'" → "He **told** me **that** he **was** busy."
- **Questions**: use *asked*; *if/whether* for yes-no questions, the *wh*-word otherwise; no *that*; statement word order; no question mark. "She said to him, 'Where do you live?'" → "She asked him **where he lived**." "He said, 'Are you ready?'" → "He asked **if I was** ready."
- **Commands and requests**: *ordered, requested, advised, urged, forbade* + *to*-infinitive. "The teacher said to the boys, 'Do not run in the corridor.'" → "The teacher **advised** the boys **not to run** in the corridor." *Forbade* already carries *not*: "forbade the boys **to run**".
- **Exclamations**: "He said, 'Alas! I have failed.'" → "He **exclaimed with sorrow that** he had failed."
- **Let us**: "She said, 'Let us start the assembly.'" → "She **suggested** (or **proposed**) **that they should** start the assembly."

School example: Direct: The Principal said, "The result will be declared tomorrow." Indirect: The Principal said that the result **would be declared the next day**.

## Vocabulary: idioms, one-word substitutions, confused words

**Summary: these are recall questions, so a short list learnt well beats a long list skimmed.**

Idioms that recur in UPSC and SSC papers:
- **turn a deaf ear**: ignore deliberately · **leave no stone unturned**: make every effort · **at loggerheads**: in strong disagreement · **take with a pinch of salt**: doubt the truth of · **a red-letter day**: a memorable day · **by leaps and bounds**: very rapidly · **in the long run**: eventually · **a bone of contention**: cause of a quarrel · **beat about the bush**: avoid the main point · **bring to book**: punish · **turn over a new leaf**: change for the better · **hit the nail on the head**: say exactly the right thing · **cut no ice**: have no effect · **at the eleventh hour**: at the last moment · **call a spade a spade**: speak bluntly · **a white elephant**: a costly, useless possession · **burn the midnight oil**: study late at night · **once in a blue moon**: very rarely · **in black and white**: in writing · **a feather in one's cap**: an achievement to be proud of · **through thick and thin**: in good times and bad · **nip in the bud**: stop at an early stage · **get the sack**: be dismissed · **a wild goose chase**: a futile search · **on the cards**: likely to happen.

One-word substitutions with a school or office flavour:
- new to a job: **novice** · does something for pleasure, not money: **amateur** · knows everything: **omniscient** · all-powerful: **omnipotent** · speech without preparation: **extempore** · list of books: **bibliography** · one's own life story: **autobiography** · uses both hands equally well: **ambidextrous** · hates mankind: **misanthrope** · loves mankind: **philanthropist** · speaks many languages: **polyglot** · short witty saying: **epigram** · government by officials: **bureaucracy** · of the same age or time: **contemporary** · cannot be corrected: **incorrigible** · cannot be read: **illegible** · disease spreading widely: **epidemic** · study of teaching methods: **pedagogy** · beautiful handwriting: **calligraphy** · agreed by all: **unanimous** · stays away from school without permission: **truant** · collection of poems: **anthology** · speaks little: **reticent** · believes easily: **credulous** · abstains from alcohol: **teetotaller** · word opposite in meaning: **antonym**.

Confused pairs (one-line contrast):
- **affect** (verb, to influence) / **effect** (noun, result)
- **advice** (noun) / **advise** (verb); **practice** (noun) / **practise** (verb) in British English
- **principal** (head of school; main) / **principle** (rule)
- **stationery** (paper, pens) / **stationary** (not moving)
- **complement** (completes) / **compliment** (praise)
- **personal** (private) / **personnel** (staff)
- **council** (a body) / **counsel** (advice; a lawyer)
- **eminent** (famous) / **imminent** (about to happen)
- **precede** (go before) / **proceed** (go on)
- **access** (entry) / **excess** (too much)
- **its** (possessive) / **it's** (it is); **lose** (verb) / **loose** (not tight)
- **farther** (distance) / **further** (additional)
- **childish** (silly) / **childlike** (innocent); **historic** (important) / **historical** (about history); **economic** (of the economy) / **economical** (thrifty)
- **ensure** (make certain) / **insure** (cover by insurance) / **assure** (tell confidently)
- **continual** (repeated with breaks) / **continuous** (without a break)
- **emigrate** (leave a country) / **immigrate** (enter a country)

Memory aid: the **principal** is your **pal**; a **principle** is a ru**le**. Station**e**ry has **e** for **envelope**.

## Sentence arrangement and comprehension

**Summary: find the opening sentence by what it introduces, then chain the rest by pronouns and linkers.**

- The **first** sentence names the topic with a full noun phrase ("A School Development Plan is...") and does not start with *it, this, they, however, therefore, but, also*.
- Chain by reference: a sentence with *this plan, the committee, it* must follow the sentence that introduced that noun.
- Chain by time and logic: *then, after that, finally, as a result, however*.
- Fix the pair you are surest of and eliminate options that break it. Two eliminations usually leave the answer.
- Comprehension: read the questions first, then the passage. Answers to "according to the passage" questions must be stated in the passage, not drawn from outside knowledge. For "title" or "main idea" questions pick the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.

## Ten solved error-spotting examples

**Summary: apply the checklist in order: subject, tense, preposition, article, pronoun, comparison.**

1. "One of the teacher has not submitted the marks." *One of* needs a plural noun: "one of the **teachers** has". Shortcut: *one of* + plural noun + singular verb.
2. "The quality of the answer sheets were poor." Subject is *quality*: "**was** poor". Shortcut: cross out the *of*-phrase, then match.
3. "He has joined the school in 2019." *In 2019* is finished time: "He **joined**". Shortcut: finished-time word → simple past.
4. "The students entered into the hall quietly." *Enter* a place takes no preposition: "**entered** the hall". Shortcut: *enter into* only for agreements.
5. "The DDO is senior than the Head Clerk." Latin comparative: "senior **to**".
6. "Neither of the two candidates were eligible." *Neither* is singular: "**was** eligible".
7. "She is more wiser than her colleague." Double comparative: "**wiser** than".
8. "The Principal asked that why I was late." Reported questions take no *that*: "asked **why** I was late".
9. "If it will rain tomorrow, the sports day will be postponed." No future in the if-clause: "If it **rains** tomorrow".
10. "He gave me an useful information." Two faults: *a useful* (sound /ju:/) and *information* is uncountable: "**a useful piece of information**".

Three transformations:
11. Active: "The committee is reviewing the fee structure." Passive: "The fee structure **is being reviewed** by the committee." (present continuous → is being + V3)
12. Direct: "She said to me, 'Have you finished the audit?'" Indirect: "She **asked me whether I had finished** the audit." (yes-no question → whether; present perfect → past perfect)
13. Direct: "The teacher said, 'Honesty is the best policy.'" Indirect: "The teacher said that honesty **is** the best policy." (universal truth, no shift)

## Common traps

- A phrase after *along with, as well as, together with* that looks like a second subject. Only *and* adds a subject.
- *The number of* (singular) swapped with *a number of* (plural).
- Present perfect with a finished-time word: "has joined in 2019", "have met him yesterday".
- An extra preposition after *discuss, enter, reach, comprise, resemble, order, attack*.
- *Than* after *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer*.
- *a/an* chosen by letter instead of sound: "a hour", "an university", "a MLA".
- Plurals of uncountables: *advices, furnitures, informations, equipments, sceneries*.
- *Would* inside an if-clause; *not* after *unless*.
- A reported question with *that* or with question word order: "asked that where was I".
- *Tomorrow, yesterday, here, now* left unchanged in indirect speech.
- *Less* with countables ("less students"); *between* with more than two; *each other* for more than two.
- "Than any city" without *other*; "more unique"; "more better".
- A sentence with no error at all. If every check passes, mark "No error".

## Remember for the exam

1. *Along with, as well as, together with, with*: the verb agrees with the first subject.
2. *Either...or, neither...nor*: the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
3. *A number of* → plural verb; *the number of* → singular verb.
4. *Each, every, everyone, nobody, either, neither, many a, more than one* → singular verb.
5. *Furniture, advice, information, news, luggage, scenery, equipment, stationery* are uncountable: no *-s*, no *a/an*, singular verb.
6. *a/an* by sound: an hour, an MLA, an FIR; a university, a European, a one-rupee note.
7. *Since* + point of time; *for* + period. No present perfect with *yesterday, ago, in 2019*.
8. Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions; present tense in time clauses after *when, until, as soon as*.
9. If + past perfect → *would have* + V3. *Would* never enters the if-clause.
10. No preposition after *discuss, enter (a place), reach, resemble, comprise, order, attack*.
11. *Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer* take *to*.
12. "Than any **other** city"; comparative for two, superlative for three or more.
13. Passive = object as subject + *be* in the same tense + V3 + *by* doer.
14. Indirect speech: shift the tense back; *will → would*; *tomorrow → the next day*; *yesterday → the previous day*; *now → then*; *here → there*.
15. Reporting verb in present or future, or a universal truth: no tense change.

quick_facts: Along with, as well as, together with, with: the verb agrees with the first subject; only 'and' adds a subject.
Either...or and neither...nor: the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
'A number of' takes a plural verb; 'the number of' takes a singular verb.
Each, every, everyone, nobody, either, neither, many a, more than one: singular verb.
Furniture, advice, information, news, luggage, scenery, equipment, stationery are uncountable: no -s, no a/an, singular verb.
a/an goes by sound: an hour, an MLA, an FIR, an NGO; a university, a European, a one-rupee note.
Since + point of time, for + period; present perfect never with yesterday, ago, last year or in 2019.
Past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions; time clauses after when, until, as soon as take the present tense.
If + past perfect pairs with would have + V3; 'would' never appears inside the if-clause; 'unless' already means 'if not'.
No preposition after discuss, enter (a place), reach, resemble, comprise, order, attack, accompany.
Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior and prefer take 'to', never 'than'.
Comparative for two, superlative for three or more; 'than any other city' needs 'other'.
Passive voice: object becomes subject + be in the same tense + past participle + by doer; present perfect becomes has/have been + V3.
Indirect speech with a past reporting verb: tense shifts back, will becomes would, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday the previous day, now then, here there.
No tense shift when the reporting verb is present or future, or when the statement is a universal truth.

mcqs.q_en:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

The Principal, along with the teachers, (A) / are attending (B) / the orientation programme at the DIET. (C) / No error (D)
mcqs.explain_en: 'Along with the teachers' is a phrase, not a second subject, so the verb agrees with 'The Principal' and must be 'is attending'. Parts A and C are correct, so 'No error' is the trap.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar: subject-verb agreement (words between subject and verb)

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct word to fill the blank.

She has been working in this school ______ 2018.
mcqs.explain_en: 'Since' marks a point of time (2018) and goes with a perfect tense. 'For' needs a period ('for seven years'), while 'from' and 'by' do not fit the present perfect continuous.

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the set of articles that correctly fills the blanks in order.

______ MLA visited our school yesterday and spent ______ hour with ______ students of Class XII.
mcqs.explain_en: MLA begins with the vowel sound /em/, so 'an MLA'; 'hour' has a silent h, so 'an hour'; the students are specified by 'of Class XII', so 'the students'. Option A fails on 'a MLA', C on 'a hour' and D on 'a students'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: articles (a/an by sound; the with specified nouns)

mcqs.q_en: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options_en: The committee have submitted its report.
The number of students in Class X are increasing.
A number of teachers have applied for the training.
Each of the students have been given a book.
mcqs.explain_en: 'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb, so C is right. 'The number of' takes a singular verb (B), 'each of' takes a singular verb (D), and A mixes the plural verb 'have' with the singular pronoun 'its'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: agreement with 'a number of', 'the number of', 'each of' and collective nouns

mcqs.q_en:
Consider the following sentences:
1. He insisted on me to attend the meeting.
2. The school comprises of three wings.
3. She is senior to me by two years.
4. We discussed about the matter in the staff meeting.

Which of the above is/are grammatically correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Only sentence 3 is correct: 'senior to'. 'Insist on' must be followed by a noun or -ing form ('insisted on my attending'), 'comprise' takes no 'of', and 'discuss' takes no 'about'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: verbs that take no preposition; Latin comparatives with 'to'

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct passive form of the sentence.

The Vice Principal has signed the attendance register.
options_en: The attendance register was signed by the Vice Principal.
The attendance register has been signed by the Vice Principal.
The attendance register had been signed by the Vice Principal.
The attendance register is signed by the Vice Principal.
mcqs.explain_en: Present perfect active ('has signed') becomes 'has/have been' + past participle in the passive. 'Was signed' is simple past, 'had been signed' is past perfect and 'is signed' is simple present, so each changes the tense.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: active and passive voice (tense table)

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct indirect form of the sentence.

He said, "I will submit the report tomorrow."
options_en: He said that he will submit the report tomorrow.
He said that he would submit the report tomorrow.
He said that he had submitted the report the next day.
He said that he would submit the report the next day.
mcqs.explain_en: With a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. Option A changes neither, B leaves 'tomorrow' unchanged, and C wrongly shifts the future to the past perfect.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: reported speech (tense shift and change of time words)

mcqs.q_en: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options_en: If he would have studied, he would have passed.
If he had studied, he would have passed.
If he studied, he would have passed.
If he has studied, he would pass.
mcqs.explain_en: An unreal past condition takes the past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have + V3' in the main clause. 'Would' never appears in the if-clause (A), and C and D mix the conditional types.

mcqs.q_en:
Assertion (A): The sentence "The furnitures in the staff room are old" is grammatically incorrect.
Reason (R): "Furniture" is an uncountable noun; it has no plural form and takes a singular verb.

Select the correct answer.
options_en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
mcqs.explain_en: Furniture is uncountable, so it has no plural and takes a singular verb: 'The furniture in the staff room is old.' The reason states exactly why the sentence is wrong.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: uncountable nouns (furniture, advice, information)

mcqs.q_en:
Match List-I (Idiom) with List-II (Meaning) and select the correct answer.

List-I
A. To turn a deaf ear
B. To leave no stone unturned
C. To be at loggerheads
D. To take with a pinch of salt

List-II
1. To make every possible effort
2. To doubt the truth of something
3. To ignore deliberately
4. To be in strong disagreement
mcqs.explain_en: To turn a deaf ear is to ignore, to leave no stone unturned is to make every effort, to be at loggerheads is to be in strong disagreement, and to take with a pinch of salt is to doubt the truth of something.
mcqs.source: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English: idioms and phrases

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the one word that substitutes the given expression.

A person who is new to a profession or activity
mcqs.explain_en: A novice is a beginner. An amateur does something for pleasure rather than as a profession, a veteran has long experience, and a connoisseur is an expert judge of taste.
mcqs.source: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English: one-word substitutions

mcqs.q_en: Which one of the following sentences uses the italicised word correctly?
options_en: The new timetable will *effect* all the sections.
The Principal gave sound *advise* to the staff.
The *stationary* for the examination has arrived.
mcqs.explain_en: In British English, which Indian examinations follow, 'practise' is the verb and 'practice' the noun, so D is correct. The others confuse affect/effect (verb needed), advice/advise (noun needed) and stationery/stationary (paper, not 'not moving').
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin / Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary: commonly confused words

mcqs.q_en:
Assertion (A): The sentence "Neither the Principal nor the teachers was present at the meeting" is grammatically correct.
Reason (R): With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it.

Select the correct answer.
options_en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
mcqs.explain_en: The nearer subject is 'the teachers' (plural), so the verb must be 'were' and the assertion is false. The reason states the rule correctly, which is exactly why the sentence fails.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: agreement with either...or / neither...nor

mcqs.q_en:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

She is one of (A) / the teachers who (B) / has been selected for the State award this year. (C) / No error (D)
mcqs.explain_en: 'Who' refers to 'the teachers' (plural), so the relative clause needs 'have been selected'. The singular would be correct only in 'the only one of the teachers who has been selected'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: agreement of the verb with the antecedent of a relative pronoun

mcqs.q_en:
Arrange the following sentences P, Q, R and S in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph.

P. Once submitted, the plan becomes the basis for the grants made by the government or the local authority.
Q. A School Development Plan is a three-year plan for a school.
R. The School Management Committee prepares this plan as three annual sub-plans.
S. The committee then submits it to the local authority.
mcqs.explain_en: Q introduces the plan with a full noun phrase; R refers back with 'this plan' and introduces the committee; S follows with 'the committee then submits it'; P ('once submitted') needs the submission in S. Option B uses 'the committee' before it is introduced, C opens with 'this plan', and D has the plan 'submitted' before S submits it.
mcqs.source: Sentence rearrangement technique (reference chains); content from RTE Act 2009 s.21-22 and RTE Rules on the School Development Plan
